# Open ADMS — Decisions

> **Looking for what's true now?** Read `agent_store/SUMMARY.md`: current rules by topic, the ADRs
> to cite, and which ones below are superseded. This file is the full history.

Executive architectural decisions, and the dated session log. **Append, never rewrite.**
New decision → new ADR row. Never renumber existing entries.
How to write one: the `adms-decisions` skill. Live code-vs-spec gaps: `agent_store/DEVIATIONS.md`.

## 🏛️ Architecture Decision Records

| ADR | Date | Area | Decision & rationale | Invariant it creates |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **ADR-001** | 2026-09-23 | Schema | ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED BY ADR-074** — debris types are a firm-extendable list, seeded with these 12; the "never free text" reason stands (picked, never typed). Original: **Hardcode the 12 USACE umbrella debris categories now**, not later. Free-text debris types are the classic source of dirty reimbursement data (`Tree`, `tree`, `Tresss`) and a late migration would rewrite every ticket table. | `DebrisType` is a closed DB enum: `CD VEG METALS CONCRETE WHITE_GOODS TITLED_PROPERTY HHM RACM SOIL LEANERS HANGERS STUMPS`. Never widened without a new ADR + migration. |
| **ADR-002** | 2026-09-23 | Architecture | **`ServiceCode` is the single customization point for billable work.** Project admins define codes and rates; they never invent debris types. | Admins set `code`, `name`, `billingUnit`, `rate` on `ServiceCode` and pick a `DebrisType` from the enum. Rates live nowhere else. |
| **ADR-003** | 2026-09-23 | Roadmap | **Field web app (Phase 3) ships before back-office (Phase 4).** Data originates in the field; validating offline capture must precede building dashboards that consume it. | `field-webapp` precedes `back-office-webapp`. |
| **ADR-004** | 2026-09-23 | Infra | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-099** — Railway + Netlify is the shipped demo deploy; firms host in their own cloud. Local-first stands. Original: **Local-first development.** Everything runs and passes green in local Docker + localhost before any cloud deploy. | Local `postgres:16-alpine` + local dev servers are the dev target. Railway/Netlify are Phase 5 production targets. |
| **ADR-005** | 2026-09-23 | Geospatial | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-094** — geodesic math lives in one TypeScript module (the rebuild has no `gps.py`); the rule stands. Original: **High-precision coordinates, geodesic math only.** Float coordinates and Euclidean shortcuts produce distance errors large enough to wrongly pass or fail a disposal-proximity check — i.e. to mis-bill. | All lat/lon are `Decimal @db.Decimal(38, 8)` (WGS84 / EPSG:4326). All distance math is geodesic and lives only in `gps.py`. |
| **ADR-006** | 2026-09-23 | Ticketing | **Split-ticket primitives in the core schema from Phase 1.** Split ticketing is a USACE requirement; retrofitting it would touch every ticket table. | Every ticket carries `isSplitTicket` (Boolean) + `splitIdentifier` (`A`, `B`, …). Zod enforces both-or-neither. |
| **ADR-007** | 2026-09-23 | Integrity | ⚠️ **`Transaction` part SUPERSEDED BY ADR-085** — transactions are regenerated when their ticket changes; `AuditRecord` stays append-only and keeps every removed transaction. Original: **Zero hard deletes; append-only ledger and audit.** Operational records are federal audit evidence for years. | `Transaction` and `AuditRecord` are append-only. Everything else soft-archives. Every mutation calls `writeAudit()` / `write_audit()`. |
| **ADR-008** | 2026-09-23 | Agent safety | **The agent never runs state-changing git commands.** Agents get trapped in git loops and can destroy uncommitted work. | No `add`/`commit`/`push`/`checkout`/`reset`/`restore`/`stash`/`clean`. Read-only inspection (`status`, `diff`, `log`, `branch --show-current`) is permitted so the agent can report accurately. Agent emits copy-paste commands; user runs them. Never commit to `main`. |
| **ADR-009** | 2026-09-23 | Schema | **Prisma has no table inheritance, so the two inheritance families use opposite strategies.** Tickets inline all base columns per concrete table (reads never join for base fields, and ticket reads dominate the workload). Certifications and submission forms keep a real parent row + discriminator + 1:1 child, because they are queried polymorphically. | Ticket base fields are duplicated per table **by design** — do not "normalise" them into a shared parent. `BaseCertification.certType` and `BaseSubmissionForm.formType` are the discriminators. |
| **ADR-010** | 2026-09-23 | Reconciliation | ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED BY ADR-019 as the pairing mechanism** — these attributes are now *validation* checks on an already-grouped pair, not how the pair is found. Retained for the reasoning about exact cert-number equality, which still holds. Original: **The ticket match key is `projectId + certNumber + zone + debrisType + timing order`, and the earliest qualifying partner wins.** A disposal consumed in a run is removed from the candidate pool. Cert number equality is exact — it is the physical-truck proof and must not be fuzzy-matched. | `_find_disposal_match` / `_find_haul_disposal_match` semantics are load-bearing. Changing the key changes what can be billed. |
| **ADR-011** | 2026-09-23 | Reconciliation | ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED BY ADR-060** — `FAILED` is dropped; every engine problem is `MANUAL_REVIEW` with a reason code. Original: **Failure severity is split by whether a machine or a person could have caused it.** GPS drift, route span and clock ordering are sensor/clock-plausible → `MANUAL_REVIEW`. Cert, debris-type, zone, load-call and rule violations are human-attributable → `FAILED`. | Escalation set is `{DISPOSAL_GPS_TOO_FAR, TIMING_OVERLAP, ROUTE_DRIFT_EXCEEDED}` for the load workflow. See **KD-03** for the haul-out asymmetry. |
| **ADR-012** | 2026-09-23 | Reconciliation | ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED BY ADR-060** — statuses are `PENDING / COMPLETED / MANUAL_REVIEW / VOID` (migration: KD-42). Original: **Implemented statuses are `PENDING / MATCHED / FAILED / MANUAL_REVIEW`.** Earlier prose referenced `HARD_REVIEW` / `SOFT_REVIEW`; those names were never implemented. Rather than migrate the enum mid-phase, the four existing values stand and the prose was corrected. | Do not introduce `HARD_REVIEW` / `SOFT_REVIEW` without an ADR and a migration. "Hard" ⇒ `FAILED`; "soft" ⇒ `MANUAL_REVIEW`. |
| **ADR-013** | 2026-09-23 | Ticketing | **The haul-out workflow carries `loadCall` on its *collection* side**, inverting the standard workflow. A haul-out container is judged full at the TDSR at load-out, which is the observable, attestable moment; a standard truck is judged at the disposal tower after settling in transit. | `HaulOutDisposalTicket` has **no** `loadCall` column and must not gain one. `compute_volume` for haul-out reads `hoc.load_call`. |
| **ADR-014** | 2026-09-23 | Agent tooling | **The agent state files are split by function and are case-sensitive UPPERCASE.** A single monolithic instruction file dilutes attention across an 80-page spec; an empty or mis-cased pointer silently yields no context at all. | `agent_store/{WORK_SPEC,CURRENT_BUILD,MEMORY,SYSTEM_REQUIREMENTS_SHEET}.md`. `WORK_SPEC.md` is immutable; the other three are agent-writable. `CLAUDE.md` / `GROK.md` are thin pointers to `AGENT.md` — one source of truth, no forked copies. |
| **ADR-015** | 2026-09-23 | Certification | **A certification certifies a CONTAINER or a CREW — not a vehicle.** What is billed is the volume of the thing that holds the debris, so that is what gets measured and numbered. A tandem dump bed, a towed trailer behind a pickup, an integral built-in bed, and a self-loader's box are all the same kind of record: a measured box with an operator, a licence, photos, and a number. The chassis is incidental. | `ContainerCertificate` = measured subject. `CrewCertificate` (bucket truck, skid steer) = unmeasured, because its work is billed per-each or per crew-day, never per CY. Swapping which pickup tows a certified trailer does **not** create a new certification; one chassis carrying two certified boxes needs **two**. |
| **ADR-016** | 2026-09-23 | Certification | ⚠️ **PARTLY SUPERSEDED BY ADR-045** — the number may also come from pre-printed certification paper; uniqueness is per project. "One identifier, never a second placard field" still holds. Original: **The cert number and the placard number are ONE identifier, system-generated.** A placard is blank laminated card stock with a space to write a number on in sharpie — consumable physical supply, not a data model. The system issues a number (e.g. `10090`) at certification time, exactly as it issues ticket numbers; that number is written on the placard and copied onto every ticket, report and ledger row. | `BaseCertification.certNumber` is the single identity, system-generated, never caller-supplied. **Never add a `truckPlacardNumber` column.** The USACE/LOADM `Truck Placard Number` export field is populated *from* `certNumber` at serialization time — a serialization concern, not a second identifier. See **KD-10**. |
| **ADR-017** | 2026-09-23 | Certification | **Tickets deliberately carry both `certId` and a copied `certNumber`.** `certId` is the referential link; `certNumber` is a frozen point-in-time snapshot of the identity the monitor saw on the placard. Tickets are evidence and must not mutate because a parent row was later edited. | The denormalization stays. Note the consequence: since `ticketService.ts` copies `certNumber` from the resolved cert, `validate_ticket_pair_cert` fires only when two monitors selected *different certifications* — a wrong-container error, not a typo. |
| **ADR-018** | 2026-09-23 | Rules | **A rule targets exactly one concrete `TicketType`, and a project declares which ticket types it enables.** Considered and rejected making rules type-agnostic or resolving type through a join: the reconciler sweeps a queue continuously, so rule dispatch must stay a direct in-memory comparison on a value already loaded — no query just to learn a type. Ticket type is a property of the concrete ticket classes, so pointing rules at them based on what a project enables is the right level. | `Rule.ticketType` stays a single `TicketType`. `Project` gains an enabled-ticket-types set (**KD-14**), and rules are authored against it. Do not "generalise" rule targeting. |
| **ADR-019** | 2026-09-23 | Reconciliation | **Pairs are matched on the TICKET NUMBER, not on a composite of ticket attributes.** Both halves of a load share one number, issued at collection and physically carried by the truck to the dump. Reconciliation is therefore a grouping operation over the queue, not an attribute search. **Ticket type is not a match input** — a pair is grouped first, then *tested* for type agreement along with cert, debris type, zone, timing and GPS. A type mismatch inside a number is a finding to report, not a reason the pair was never found. | Supersedes the composite match key in ADR-010 *as the pairing mechanism*; those attributes remain **validation** checks on a grouped pair (§5.1). Implementation diverges — see **KD-12**, **KD-13**. |
| **ADR-020** | 2026-09-23 | Data integrity | ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED BY ADR-039 and ADR-051** — every captured field is correctable by permission, not only `ticketNumber`. The renumber-and-requeue flow still stands. Original: **An authorised reviewer may correct `ticketNumber` on a ticket in `MANUAL_REVIEW`, and nothing else.** Offline sync means keying errors (e.g. one barcode scanned twice at disposal) surface hours later as a ticket number carrying three records. The engine must never guess which disposal belongs to which collection; a human deduces it from cert number, times, GPS and photos and repairs the identifier. Rationale for allowing exactly this field: the number is the only thing on a ticket that is *assigned to* the load rather than *observed*. Everything else is testimony and is never edited. | Sole carve-out to invariant 5. Audited with the prior number retained, reviewer's user id (never `SYSTEM`), only from `MANUAL_REVIEW`, never on a `MATCHED` or billed ticket. The reviewer renumbers and returns the records to `PENDING` — they never force a match or author a `LoadTicket`. |
| **ADR-021** | 2026-09-23 | Ticketing | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-046** — numbers are bare (no prefixes of any kind), which withdraws the reconciled records' `LDT-`/`HOT-` identity; whether they carry the load's number or their own is open (Q-51). The rest stands. Original: **The ticket number is generated once at COLLECTION, is stage-neutral, and is scanned (never regenerated) at disposal. `@unique` per stage table stands.** User decision. The number is printed/barcoded onto the ticket the truck carries, so the same value appears at most once as a collection and once as a disposal — exactly the shape of one load. The constraint is the database's guarantee that one load cannot be dumped twice under one number: a duplicate is **rejected at the sync boundary** and never enters the reconciliation queue. | Generator drops the per-type prefix and is called only on the collection-side create paths (`CollectionTicket`, `HaulOutCollectionTicket`, `UnitRateTicket`). Disposal capture takes the number as input. The existing `@unique` constraints are correct and stay — **KD-13 is a generator and capture-path change, not a constraint change.** Reconciled `LoadTicket`/`HaulOutTicket` keep their own generated `LDT-`/`HOT-` identity. |
| **ADR-022** | 2026-09-23 | Data integrity | **A sync payload rejected for a duplicate ticket number is quarantined in full, never dropped, and never acknowledged to the device as saved.** A rejected record is a monitor's observation of real work; discarding it destroys evidence and leaves a legitimate load permanently unbilled — the same failure the system exists to prevent, reached from the opposite direction. | Rejected records persist with their rejection reason and the id of the record holding the number, and surface in a review queue where a reviewer applies the ADR-020 renumber. Follows from ADR-021: the constraint protects the ledger, the quarantine protects the evidence. |
| **ADR-023** | 2026-09-23 | Org model | **Three distinct layers: `Client` → `DeclarationEvent` → `Project`(`programType`).** They are routinely conflated because speech calls all of them "the job", but they answer different questions and have different lifetimes. A client is long-lived and reused across disasters; an event is one declaration (`DR-4673-FL` or a state/local/internal reference — **not always a FEMA number**); a project is one body of work under that event, typed by `programType`. | Operators **select an existing client** rather than re-creating one. One event drives many projects (a county's ROW, PPDR and waterway work under one DR). See **KD-16**. |
| **ADR-024** | 2026-09-23 | Org model | **`programType` on `Project` is behavioural, not a label.** Confirmed values: `ROW`, `PARKS`, `PPDR`, `WATERWAY`. It determines whether a signed ROE is required before work on a parcel — private-property work without one is a trespass and an unreimbursable cost, while public right-of-way work needs none. | `requireRoe` stops being a `Program` flag and becomes derived from `programType`: required for `PPDR` (and `CPDR` if adopted), not for `ROW`/`PARKS`/`WATERWAY`. Candidate additional types are **unconfirmed** — see **KD-17**. |
| **ADR-025** | 2026-09-23 | Data integrity | ⚠️ **PARTLY SUPERSEDED BY ADR-039 and ADR-051** — operational records are correctable by permission too, GPS included. Still true: reference data is ordinary audited admin work, and nothing is hard-deleted. Original: **Reference data is editable; operational evidence is not.** Conflating them makes agents wrongly block ordinary admin work. A client's contact details, a contractor's phone number, a service code's forward rate are standing facts about the world that legitimately change; a ticket is testimony about what someone observed at a moment in time. | "No hard deletes" applies to both populations. "Never changes after creation" applies **only** to tickets, certifications, `Transaction` and `AuditRecord`. Editing reference data is expected and audited; editing a ticket's GPS is never permitted. See §3.1b. |
| **ADR-026** | 2026-09-23 | Org model | **`Client` and `DeclarationEvent` are shared, global, first-class objects — referenced, not contained.** User decision, resolving the open question under ADR-023. An event is created once, searchable in its own right, and referenced by any number of projects across any number of clients; `DR-4673-FL` is recorded once and every affected county's project points at the same record. | The §4.0 setup order (client → event → project) is the sequence an **operator works in**, not a containment hierarchy. Selecting an existing event is as ordinary as selecting an existing client. **Good news for KD-16:** today's FK shape (`Project.clientId` + `Project.programId`) is already correct — `Program` becomes `DeclarationEvent` and `programType` moves onto `Project`. |
| **ADR-027** | 2026-09-23 | Ticketing | **One truck has exactly one open load at a time.** It loads, drives, dumps, then returns to the route. Collections and disposals for a single cert therefore interleave, and **two open collections on one cert with overlapping load windows is physically impossible.** User correction to a worked example that had violated this. | Load this into any reasoning about ticket sequences. It is also a **detection rule**: overlapping collections on one cert with no intervening disposal means duplicate issuance (§4.3a Scenario B), not two loads. |
| **ADR-028** | 2026-09-23 | Reconciliation | **A phantom ticket is VOIDED, never renumbered.** Renumbering a record that describes work which does not separately exist manufactures a second load out of one pile and invites someone to find it a disposal partner — double-billing by way of a data fix. | Renumber (ADR-020) only for **real work wearing the wrong identifier** (Scenario A). Void for a record of work that never happened (Scenario B). Establish which scenario applies *before* touching a ticket number. |
| **ADR-029** | 2026-09-23 | Reconciliation | ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED BY ADR-053** — no grace period and no ageing; an unpartnered half never expires (preloads are common). Still true: arrival order means nothing, and `PENDING` is never alerted on. Original: **Orphan detection is age-based and measured in FIELD time, never on arrival.** ⚠️ *Revised — the original rationale (that disposal sites have wifi while field tablets do not) was wrong; see ADR-030.* The correct reason is stronger: the whole operation syncs at EOD in whatever order devices connect, so a batch of unpartnered records is the ordinary shape of a sync. Alerting on arrival produces dozens of false alarms daily, and a queue that cries wolf every day is one nobody reads — exactly how the real orphan slips through. | `PENDING` is **not** an error state and is never alerted on directly. Age from `loadEndTime` / `disposalStartTime` — never from server `createdAt` — with a threshold tolerant of a device dark for days. |
| **ADR-030** | 2026-09-23 | Architecture | ⚠️ **Consequence (b) SUPERSEDED BY ADR-053** — there are no grace periods. (a), (c) and (d) stand. Original: **The ENTIRE field operation is offline and syncs at end of day — the disposal site included.** User correction. A TDSR is a cleared field or gravel lot stood up for the response: no fibre, no reliable cell, often no mains power. Assuming the disposal tower is an always-connected node is the most dangerous assumption available here, because every real-time control designed on top of it does not exist. | Four consequences, all load-bearing: **(a)** arrival order carries no information — never infer sequence or suspicion from server `createdAt`; order by field timestamps. **(b)** Grace periods are measured in field time and must tolerate multi-day device gaps. **(c)** Old work arrives behind new work — the queue is **not monotonic**; a late arrival is not suspicious. **(d)** Load is bursty: idle all day, then a full operation in minutes. Size for the spike. |
| **ADR-031** | 2026-09-23 | Field app | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-071** — disposal devices carry no ticket list (they trust the scan); their truck list is best-effort. Original: **Nothing can be validated in the field; on-device checks are advisory only.** The disposal tablet is offline at the gate, so it cannot confirm a scanned number exists, is open, or was not already used by another device. This is precisely why a mis-scan reaches the database and why the sync-boundary rejection is where the defence lives. | Still build: **local duplicate detection** against the device's own buffer (catches the common same-monitor-twice case cheaply), and a **cached project manifest** (active certs, enabled ticket types, open numbers as of last sync). The manifest is **stale by construction** — a mismatch prompts the monitor, never hard-blocks. Blocking on stale data strands legitimate work in the field, which is worse than letting the server sort it out. |
| **ADR-032** | 2026-09-23 | Ticketing | **Split tickets are for PPDR/ROE work — N collections to ONE disposal, not one collection to N destinations.** User correction. Trucks do not mix debris streams across destinations in real operations despite USACE guidance allowing it. What actually happens: a loader works several ROE properties into one load, and the load is split into one ticket per property so volume can be attributed to the parcel it came from. | Shape is **N:1**. Each split carries a distinct suffixed number (`10095-A`…`-E`), so `@unique` per stage table is **never violated** — the conflict recorded in the first draft of KD-19 did not exist and came from an inverted reading. The driver carries **one** barcode, the base number, because there is one physical load. |
| **ADR-033** | 2026-09-23 | Reconciliation | **Grouping keys on the BASE ticket number, with any `-A`..`-Z` suffix stripped.** Grouping on the literal string would give N groups of one and reconcile nothing. A valid group is N collections (N≥1) + exactly one disposal; N=1 is the ordinary unsplit load. | Two disposals on one base number, a gap in the suffix sequence, or a suffixed collection with no chain remain ambiguous → `MANUAL_REVIEW`. Split members must share cert, debris type and zone. |
| **ADR-034** | 2026-09-23 | Evidence | **A scale receipt is modelled as its own record, not as columns on a ticket.** ⚠️ *Scope of its evidentiary value later tempered by ADR-038 — only a professional weighing is independent evidence; a handwritten receipt-book slip is a lineage token.* Hanging `grossWeightLbs`/`netWeightTons` off `DisposalTicket` would duplicate one physical weighing across the two tickets of a tandem and invite summing them — billing 34.2 tons for a 17.1-ton load. | Its number is **captured, not generated** (first external identifier in the system — contrast ADR-016 and ADR-021): stored verbatim, never normalised, never regenerated. One receipt references N tickets. **Consumable exactly once** — unique per project; reuse on a later trip is a direct double-billing vector. |
| **ADR-035** | 2026-09-23 | Billing | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-175** — a shared weight is apportioned by certified capacity, and both tickets are flagged. **Where billing is by TON, a combined scale weight is apportioned by LOAD-CALLED VOLUME**, not evenly and not by certified capacity — only load-called volume reflects what each container actually carried. The apportioned figure is **derived, never observed**: on a tandem, only the combined net was ever weighed. | Computed server-side and deterministically like `compute_volume()`; never accepted from a client. **Observed and derived figures are stored separately** so the audit trail can answer "weighed, or inferred?" years later. Rounding must neither create nor destroy tonnage — `Σ apportioned` equals the scale net exactly. Where `billingUnit` is `CY` the receipt is corroboration, not the billed quantity. |
| **ADR-036** | 2026-09-23 | Evidence | **Whether a scale receipt exists is decided by DESTINATION; whether it matters is decided by the CONTRACT.** User model. A load ending at a **TDSR/DMS never produces one** — there is no scale at a field staging site. Only an **FDS** can. Given an FDS: if the contract bills by CY the receipt is **optional** and captured purely as a chain-of-custody token proving the load arrived, with **zero a legitimate weight**; if it bills by TON the receipt is **required** and its weight is the billed quantity. | "Missing" is the normal case far more often than it is a fault — never validate scale data unconditionally. `DisposalSite.siteType` (`TDRS` vs `FDS`) already distinguishes destinations. Whether `DMS` needs to be a distinct enum value is a schema decision, not a synonym to paper over. |
| **ADR-037** | 2026-09-23 | Rules | **The scale-data requirement is declared on the `ServiceCode` and tested through a `SCALE_NUMBER` rule condition.** It follows the money, so it belongs where rates live (ADR-002): the contract's billing basis decides, the service code carries the flag, the linked rule carries a `SCALE_NUMBER` condition the reconciler tests. | New rule condition key (§5.3, previously an exhaustive list). Scale data exists only at disposal, so the check runs on a **grouped pair** and never blocks pairing. Missing-when-required → `MANUAL_REVIEW`, **not `FAILED`** — untranscribed paperwork is not an eligibility violation. |
| **ADR-038** | 2026-09-23 | Evidence | **A scale receipt's evidentiary weight depends on which kind of document it is, and a "tandem" is not a modelled concept.** Two corrections. (a) A professional weighing off calibrated equipment is genuinely independent evidence; a handwritten receipt-book slip from a connex-box "scale house" is a lineage token asserting nothing about quantity. An earlier draft called every receipt the strongest evidence in the record — overstated. (b) **Nothing in the data says two containers travelled together.** The system sees independently certified containers with independent tickets; the receipt, linked by a monitor, is the *only* place that pairing exists. | Never build logic treating every receipt as an authoritative measurement. Never infer a tandem — if a trailer has no ticket, the system cannot know it was there and must not guess. Receipts are **transcribed by hand, never scanned**, so duplicates arrive as transcription errors. |
| **ADR-039** | 2026-09-23 | Data integrity | **Records are correctable in place by permission; immutability lives in the audit ledger, not in the record.** User decision, superseding the narrower "one carve-out" rule. A sufficiently privileged user may edit tickets, certifications, projects, incidents, surveys and synced pending tickets, **provided every edit writes an `AuditRecord` carrying the prior value under the real human's id**. Spawning a replacement object for every authorized correction fragments one real-world thing across many rows and forces every reader to walk a chain to find current truth; editing in place keeps one row per real thing and puts history where history belongs. | Nothing is lost — prior values live in the ledger in perpetuity, so "what did this say before, and who changed it" stays answerable forever. **`Transaction` and `AuditRecord` remain append-only, absolutely** — it is *because* the ledger is immutable that everything else can safely be corrected. A monitor still cannot edit their own submitted ticket in the field. Correction ≠ void: void still applies where the work never happened (ADR-028). |
| **ADR-040** | 2026-09-23 | Ticketing | **Unit rate capture shape and billing basis are independent.** HHW is captured as an itemized breakdown and billed **by the pound**; white goods are captured the same way and billed **per item**. The ticket records what was collected; `ServiceCode` + `Rule` decide what it is worth. Refrigerant recovery is a separate billable action from the appliance (`fridge_w_freon` and `freon_extracted` both appear). | Never infer billing basis from capture shape. Itemized ≠ per-item. Hangers and stumps need only an integer; HHW and white goods need a key→integer map, stored as **JSONB** because the item vocabulary is contract-defined and must grow without a migration. ⚠️ Not licence to put closed system vocabularies (`DebrisType`, statuses) in JSON. |
| **ADR-041** | 2026-09-23 | Ticketing | **The unit-count requirement is a flag on `ServiceCode`; the unit rate SUB-TYPE is declared at project setup.** Two different decisions at two different levels. `ServiceCode.requireUnitCount` (already present, `@default(false)`) is a checkbox set when a code is created — never a default, never project setup. Separately, enabling `UNIT_RATE` on a project must declare *which kinds* (hangers, leaners, stumps, HHW, white goods), because that governs what may be created before any service code or rule exists. | **`ServiceCode` stays decoupled from ticket types** — it carries no `ticketType` and must not gain one. A code is of a single type and applies to whatever it is linked to, and that link is made in a `Rule` (which carries both `serviceCodeId` and `ticketType`). Correct as built. Sub-types extend the enabled-ticket-types concept (KD-14) so `UNIT_RATE` enablement carries a set, not a boolean. |
| **ADR-042** | 2026-09-24 | Agent tooling | **Agent context is restructured onto the `AGENTS.md` + Agent Skills model, superseding ADR-014.** A single always-on `AGENT.md` of 304 lines plus a mandatory 2,017-line `WORK_SPEC.md` read cost ~56k tokens per session before any work began. Domain truth now lives in on-demand skills under `.claude/skills/`, whose descriptions (~20 tokens each) are the only always-on cost; `AGENTS.md` carries operating rules and a routing table; `database/AGENTS.md` carries rules scoped to that tree. `WORK_SPEC.md` was split verbatim — a concatenation diff proved byte-identity before deletion. | Root `AGENTS.md` stays under ~150 lines. Domain facts live in exactly one skill each and are never duplicated into `AGENTS.md`. `CLAUDE.md` is a symlink, never a second source. New domain knowledge goes to the owning skill, not to `AGENTS.md`. |
| **ADR-043** | 2026-09-24 | Agent tooling | **A `spec/` layer defines the finished product, and the hard rules are enforced mechanically instead of being text alone.** Two gaps, one change. (1) Skills say *why and what the rules are*, and `agent_store/` says *where we are*, but nothing said *what the finished system is or how to prove it's finished*, so an agent could build every part correctly and still miss the whole. `spec/` at the repo root holds `VISION.md` now, and journeys, acceptance scenarios (`AC-…` IDs) and a golden mission with an expected ledger next. It sits at the root, not in `agent_store/`, because it's a stable definition rather than session-to-session state. (2) Anthropic's guidance is that CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md is context, not enforcement. `.claude/settings.json` `permissions.deny` plus the PreToolUse `.claude/hooks/guard.sh` now enforce ADR-008 and the write boundaries (`development/`, migrations SQL, vendored dirs). | Spec content is **drafted by the agent and approved by the user section by section**; approved content is user-owned exactly like a skill (never "corrected" — log a KD). Unapproved ⚠️/❓ items are never built from. `AGENTS.md` carries a ≤15-line "What we're building" summary that must agree with `VISION.md`. The guard hook and `AGENTS.md` must be changed together; never weaken either unless the user asks. Known limits: the hook matches on the whole command string, so it over-blocks read-only git forms (stash list, tag -l) **and any command whose text merely mentions a mutating git subcommand**, e.g. a heredoc writing prose about git — write such prose with Edit/Write instead. It does not see writes made through Bash (`sed -i`, redirection). |

The register gives each question an ID and a status — ✅ answered (with source), 🔨 decided-not-built (with KD), ❓ open (what's known, what it blocks). `.claude/hooks/session-start.sh` prints the Next Atomic Task and every ❓ heading (~470 tokens), making orientation deterministic instead of depending on the agent choosing to read files. | Before asking the user how the system behaves: load the owning skill (no permission needed), then check the register. When the user answers, the answer goes into the owning skill (with the user's go-ahead) or an ADR, and the entry flips to ✅. Keep the `### ❓ Q-NN — …` heading format; the hook greps for it. |

| **ADR-060** | 2026-09-24 | Reconciliation | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-118** — a rule's Void Ticket action may also void (audited, rule named). ⚠️ **Consequences (2)–(3) SUPERSEDED BY ADR-085** — no reversing rows; a ticket's transactions are deleted and regenerated (void: deleted). Reprocessing is idempotent: if the amount hasn't changed, no rows are written. **(3)** Voiding a billed ticket writes reversing rows so it nets to zero; unvoiding and reprocessing bills it again. **(4)** Flagged pairs get their reconciled record too. When a correction breaks up a pair, that record is corrected in place, or voided with its source links released (prior values stay in the audit log), so the unique FKs still mean "one live bill per source ticket". **(5)** Reports separate "billed, clear" from "billed, open issue" by joining on the ticket's status; ledger rows never carry a status. | Supersedes ADR-011's `FAILED`/`MANUAL_REVIEW` split and ADR-012's status set, and ADR-048's "doesn't bill until a person has looked". | **ADR-076** | 2026-09-24 | Certification | **Container capacity follows the paper form's math exactly.** User confirmation (Q-68, in `spec/LISTS.md`): "after the primary, box 1-N can be additions or deductions … list a feature with its measurement and mark if it's an addition or subtraction and what kind of math used (divided by 2 or not?) … That math and understanding has to be perfect." **The method:** all measurements in **whole inches**. Primary V₁ = L × W × H. Each box i = 1…N: Vᵢ = L × W × H, halved when marked ÷2, **added or subtracted** as marked, labelled with a feature/type (A box shape, B sideboards, C tail gate extension, D dog box, E wheel wells, F other). Round bottom: [π × (D ÷ 2)² × L] ÷ 2, added or subtracted. The one USACE-specific capture is an **optional "USACE approved" flag on the load call**, available on any project. | **ADR-078** | 2026-09-24 | Certification | **Capacity rounding and constants: π = 3.14; round to hundredths after each step; certified capacity to the nearest whole CY with .5 up; no manual override.** User decisions (Q-68). π is 3.14 so the system matches a hand-calculated sheet. | **ADR-081** | 2026-09-24 | Billing / org | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-108** — several primes per project; subs recorded at certification under their prime. **Pricing belongs to the prime; subs work under the prime's rate; the contract sets who is prime and who is a sub, in tiers; each transaction records the prime + sub link.** User decisions (Q-70, Q-73). Adding a contract means selecting or adding its contractors and setting the prime and the subs' tiers. A service code is priced for a prime ("the rate for prime XYZ"). A rule ties a service code to a contract and the order it bills under. The user said "transaction order 1 under contract 123"; the agent reads this as the existing `Rule.transactionNumber` field. A ticket that passes the rule produces **one** transaction at the prime's rate that **records both the prime and the operating sub**. Never a prefix. **(2) Hoist / dog house:** a box may take **two lengths**; the system computes (L₁ + L₂) ÷ 2 × W × H, rounded per step. **(3) Rounding:** each step to hundredths first, so 32.495 → 32.50; then whole CY with .5 up, so → **33**. | Nothing about a modification is encoded in the cert number (ADR-046 spirit). | **ADR-085** | 2026-09-24 | Billing / ledger | **The transaction ledger shows the current truth: when a ticket changes, its transactions are deleted and regenerated. | **ADR-086** | 2026-09-24 | Reconciliation | **Any ticket can be corrected and reprocessed, including a completed one; the engine must handle a group that already has a reconciled record and transactions.** User requirement (`VISION.md` §4.6). On the next run the engine re-validates the group and **updates the existing reconciled record in place** (or voids it and releases its source links if the pair no longer holds, ADR-060 (4)), then regenerates its transactions (ADR-085). | **ADR-087** | 2026-09-24 | Certification / billing | **Radius corner box, and three crew-hour conversions, locked.** User decisions (Q-78, Q-81), accepting the agent's proposals. **Radius corner** (drawn on the USACE sheet's plan view: rounded bed corners, not a round bottom): measure L, W and H as if square; R = distance from the imaginary square corner (where straightedges along the two walls cross) to where the curve starts; run = how far the corner goes (bed height from above, bed length for a rounded floor edge); number of corners. Removed volume = (R × R − 3.14 × R × R ÷ 4) × run × corners, always subtracted, rounded to hundredths each step. Example: R 12, run 60, 2 corners → 3,715.20 cu in. **Crew hours → quantity**, set on the service code: per hour (hours); per day exact (hours ÷ day length, default 12); per day in admin-set steps (e.g. 1.5–4.5 h = 0.25 …). | Box shapes are now complete: rectangle, ÷2 triangle, two-length hoist, round bottom, radius corner. | **ADR-089** | 2026-09-24 | Billing | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-118** — the conflict key is the transaction #, not the fee kind. ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-109** — pricing is written as rule actions (Create Transaction #, contract or the ticket's contract, service code). **Pricing mechanism approved: rules match tickets and name what they bill; one transaction per matching rule; exactly one rule per fee kind.** User approval of the Q-20 proposal, point by point, plus Q-83. **Where pricing comes from:** the firm reads the **line items off the paper contract** and enters them by hand as service codes with rates, then writes rules and attaches them to the contract. **A rule** has **match** conditions (ticket type, prime, debris type, unit rate sub-type, item, zone) that say which tickets it prices, and optional **require** conditions (e.g. `load_call_min`) checked only on the tickets it matches. | **ADR-177** | 2026-09-27 | Unit rate / measurement | **The monitor records whether they measured the circumference or the diameter; rules test the diameter.** User decisions (Q-171): "(B) we must measure the tree before it is cut and it must be measured at chest height. if the tree was already cut, the monitor is able to document the diameter and take photos like normal and complete the ticket as normal and it is eligble. | **ADR-178** | 2026-09-27 | Unit rate / stumps | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-183** — from the USACE guide: only the diameter is recorded; CY rounded half up to one decimal. **A stump's volume in CY comes from its diameter by the user's formula.** User answer (Q-172), verbatim: "CY = [ (D^2 x 0.7854) x L + (RBD^2 x 0.7854) x RBH ] / 46656 where D = stump diameter in inches measured two feet up, RBD = D x 3.6 (the 1:3.6 ratio), RBH = 31 inches, 0.7854 = pi/4, 46656 = cubic inches per cubic yard." With the user's note: "the attachment never states `L`… Solving `L` back out of the published values gives **L = 24 inches**, which reproduces all 17 sampled table rows (D = 6 through 84) to 1 decimal with zero mismatches. Agent check of the formula: D = 6 → 0.258, 12 → 1.032, 24 → 4.128, 30 → 6.450, 36 → 9.289, 84 → 50.572 CY (unrounded). Lives once, in the shared domain package, with the constants named. What the ticket records, rounding, how it's paid and how the stump reaches disposal: **Q-177**. |

(5) **FEMA, read online (IS-1000 Category A, Stump Removal):** per-stump reimbursement only when the stump is **2 ft or larger in diameter measured 2 ft above the ground** and extraction is part of the service; a stump with **50% or more of the root ball exposed** may be eligible for removal and filling the hole; the removal cost is to encompass "extraction, transport, disposal, and filling the root-ball hole"; smaller stumps are paid by volume or weight. **No source found says how the fill quantity is measured.** (6) **Open, round 20:** the stump ticket's kind, fields and fill formula (**Q-189**); whether a load of stumps still bills its CY when the per-stump price already covers transport (**Q-190**, money). (7) At the user's request the agent cross-examined the whole rate sheet: **`spec/RATE-SHEET.md`** (draft), with Q-191…Q-194 for what today's setup can't express. The stump CY (ADR-178, ADR-183) stands for the load of stumps (ADR-189, ADR-192) until Q-190 is answered. Amends ADR-187, ADR-189, ADR-192. |

| **ADR-227** | 2026-09-29 | Field capture / setup / scale receipts | **What a site's phones ask for is worked out ahead by the back office from the project's rules, and follows the truck's prime.** For each site, debris class and prime, the system reads the rules on that form that could match there (the site's fee Services left out, ADR-224) and the Unit of Measure of the Services they pay: all per ton or pound → the scale receipt (number and weight) instead of a load call; anything else (per CY, a mix, or no rule) → **the load call**. | **ADR-236** | 2026-09-29 | Model / reconciliation / terms | **What a monitor records under a ticket number is a field event; everything the system writes is a conclusion drawn from events.** The user, in chat, verbatim: "If we have a load being collected and we issues a ticket with a number (whether by scanning a control ticket that was pre printed, or by generating a number) that number carries to the next site. So a collection monitor "makes" a number for a disposal monitor who calls the loads size from a tower. And a haulout collection monitor also "makes" a number and calls the loads size from a tower, for a disposal monitor who later checks to make sure the load is empty. So in the end we have Event "collection" for ticket #12345, and Event "disposal" for ticket #12345. We basically have things setup simliar to this but we aren't calling them events. And I think if you think step by step through what we have thus far-events are better? If you agree make changes so when AGENTS use skills to build this they know how to make Events instead." The agent agrees: the approved architecture already works this way (evidence inserted by sync, derived records by the worker only, jobs, idempotent and deterministic runs: ARCHITECTURE §2, §9, §13), without the word. (1) **A field event** is one monitor's record of one thing witnessed at one place and time, under a ticket number. Kinds: collection `COL`, disposal `DIS`, haul-out collection `HOC`, haul-out disposal `HOD`, unit rate `URT` (the display labels become the kinds' labels). (2) **A ticket is its number and the events recorded under it**, keyed by project + workflow + bare number (ADR-019). The first event makes the number (control ticket scanned or a generated one shown) and the truck carries it to the second. (3) **Each workflow is fixed in code** as its events, the one that makes the number and the one that takes the quantity: load `COL` → `DIS` (load call or weight at the disposal; a split has one `COL` per suffix); haul-out `HOC` → `HOD` (load call at the TDSR; the disposal confirms it dumped and left empty; ADR-013, 027); unit rate, one `URT`. A load that carries tickets lists them on its collection event and the tower counts them (ADR-192, 204). (4) **One event of each kind per ticket** (one collection per split suffix); another is the duplicate quarantined at sync (ADR-022). (5) Events arrive in any order and on any day; the engine orders by field time; a ticket missing an event is `PENDING` and never expires (ADR-030, 053). (6) **The completed load and haul-out, statuses, flags, zone, mileage and transactions are not events**: the worker draws them from the ticket's current events and the current setup, writes them alone, and draws them again on every reprocess. (7) **Event-driven processing:** a synced, back-office-created (ADR-156) or corrected event, and a setup change (ADR-090), each queue reconciliation of the tickets they touch (ARCHITECTURE §13, unchanged). (8) **Agent default: event-driven, not event-sourced.** A correction still updates the event in place with the prior value in `AuditRecord` (ADR-051, 097); there are no correction events and no state rebuilt by replaying a log, because the audit log already keeps every prior value and the approved grants (ARCHITECTURE §5) stay as they are. (9) **Agent default: forms and certifications are records, not a ticket's events** (ROE, surveys, incidents, drop-off logs never pair or bill). (10) **Words:** "field event" or its kind; never a bare "event" where the disaster could be meant (always "declaration event"); "half", "halves", "a lone half" retire. **Code (agent default, `spec/DATA-MODEL.md` may refine):** one `FieldEvent` model with `kind` `COLLECTION` · `DISPOSAL` · `HAUL_OUT_COLLECTION` · `HAUL_OUT_DISPOSAL` · `UNIT_RATE`, shared columns plus kind-specific ones checked by the kind; derived records `CompletedLoad`, `CompletedHaulOut` (ARCHITECTURE §2's historical `LoadTicket` / `HaulOutTicket` retire). | **Invariant 21:** field events are the evidence; the system's records are conclusions from them, written only by the worker and drawn again on every reprocess. No rule changes: statuses, pairing, flags, corrections, pricing stand. Done in the same response: `adms-domain` §1.2, §1.6, glossary, invariant 21; CONVENTIONS §2–§3; SUMMARY; `AGENTS.md`; ARCHITECTURE §2 (note); `BACKLOG.md` 0.2c brief (each rewrite writes in events); `NEXT.md`. The other skills and spec pages move to the words as each is rewritten. |

| **ADR-240** | 2026-09-29 | Devices / dispatch | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-477** — (6) is overturned: nothing a monitor submitted is reopened, and there is no edit log. **A phone is enrolled once; each day's assignment, written by the back office on a dispatch board, carries what a phone's setup used to: the person, the project, the work and the site.** In chat the agent reimagined phone setup from first principles; the user: "i love this because its way smarter than doing all the mental gymnastics and backend math we imagined before, and it solves a lot of the headaches at nightly checkout. It also solves natively a big issue with daily dispatching of users for work which gets tracked on a spreadsheet." Then: "if you like the "shape" of these changes to make Open ADMS more succinct and usable then go ahead and update the files". (1) **Enrol a phone once** (online, master passcode): it makes its device key (ARCHITECTURE §7.4) and joins the firm's phones; no project, no monitor. (2) **Dispatch:** the back office writes each day's **assignments** on a **dispatch board** (replacing the spreadsheet): a person, a date, a project, their work (ticket types; unit rate pay items, ADR-127; certifying, ADR-151), **one site** where the work is at one (ADR-195), optionally a phone; yesterday's board can be copied. (3) **Start of day:** the monitor signs in on any enrolled phone with Monitor ID + password (ADR-105, 120); online, the phone receives **their assignment**, its project's lists and numbers (ADR-065). No master passcode, no picking. **One assignment on a phone at a time, so one project** (ADR-145 stands). (4) **Unassigned:** the master passcode opens setup on the phone as before (project, work, site, monitor from the login list): online, or offline on the project whose lists the phone already holds (a new project needs a connection, as before); it's recorded as an **unplanned assignment**, marked, and appears on the board at sync. Switching monitors (ADR-120), the temporary session and moving site (ADR-195) work as before and amend the phone's assignment the same way; a phone keeps the login list and lists of its last assignment's project, so offline switching still works. (5) **Sync whenever there's a connection**, records first, photos after (ARCHITECTURE §9, unchanged); a phone needn't be handed in for its work to arrive. "Sync and turn in" stays for taking a phone out of service (ADR-096, 134). (6) **Agent default: a finished field event can be reopened until the monitor ends the shift** (ADR-072 said "until it syncs", which was the evening; the window stays the same). An edit to an event already sent travels as the phone's edit log, is written to `AuditRecord` under the monitor (ARCHITECTURE §9 step 8) and reprocesses the ticket; after the shift only permitted people correct (ADR-051). (7) **Every field event records its assignment and the setup version** of the lists it was captured with (the manifest is numbered), so a reviewer sees what the phone showed; the engine still draws conclusions from the current setup (ADR-236). (8) **Flag, never block:** an assignment never expires or stops field work; work under an unplanned assignment is marked, not flagged. The board shows planned against actual (assigned with no field events; a site with field events and nobody assigned) as views, not ticket flags. (9) **Not taken** from the chat, with the reason: per-person passkeys or biometrics (a phone passes between monitors in a day), device attestation (depends on Apple and Google services; self-hosted), personal phones, signed time-boxed credentials, per-supervisor keys instead of the one master passcode (ADR-106 stands). | **A phone is enrolled once; what it may make comes from its current assignment.** Amends ADR-095 (setup → enrol + assignment) and ADR-072 (reopen window); REQ-020, 311…313 revised, REQ-417 (dispatch board) added. Stands: ADR-096, 105, 106, 120, 134, 145, 151, 195. ARCHITECTURE §7–§9 are approved: the changed parts carry an ADR-240 note, for the user's approval, which doesn't block building (ADR-230). |
| **ADR-241** | 2026-09-29 | Time clock | **The time clock belongs to an assignment: anyone with one clocks in and out by hand, with simple nudges; activity is pre-filled from the field events; a manager approves the day; the hours are exported for payroll and client billing.** The user, in chat, answering the agent: "1. pays from them and bills client for hours - assumed right the need to export, 2. anyone with an assignment 3. to start just make it manual makes sense, but suggest like if they start work but aren't time in right? simple stuff nothing complex". (1) **Optional per project** (ADR-063); **anyone with an assignment** (ADR-240) has one, on the phone or, for back-office staff, in the back office. (2) **Manual:** clock in, a break (start and end), clock out. **Simple nudges, never a block:** starting a field event while not clocked in ("You're not clocked in. (3) **Activity lines are pre-filled from the day's field events** (REQ-310); the worker edits them and approves at clock-out; what the app can't know (travel, standby, training) is picked from a firm list, with a note. (4) **A manager approves each person's day**; an approved day is locked, and unlocking is audited. (5) **Exported** for the firm's payroll and for billing the client for monitors' hours. **Agent default:** Open ADMS holds no hourly rates and no pay: hours only, like the client package assembled outside it. (6) Unchanged (ADR-100): a day ends before midnight in the project's time zone, later work goes on the next day; no cap on hours; the device clock is the recorded time, checked for sense; ICS-214 data held, the form not generated. (7) **Never linked to crew time** (a unit rate ticket's item hours, ADR-084): separate records, no shared field, no cross-check (ADR-063). (8) **Agent default:** read-only viewers don't see anyone's hours; the firm sends approved hours to the client from the export. | **Time-clock entries belong to an assignment and are never linked to crew time.** Amends ADR-063 (monitors → anyone with an assignment); REQ-310 revised. | **ADR-263** | 2026-09-29 | Scaffold / local stack | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-282** — six services: the routing and address servers joined, reached through Caddy. **`infra/local` is one docker compose project, `open-adms-local`, run through a small helper: `pnpm local:up`, `local:down`, `local:wipe`, `local:status`. The historical root `docker-compose.yml` is never used (KD-59). (2) **Services:** `postgres`, `objectstore` (SeaweedFS), `mail` (Mailpit), `caddy`; images in ADR-264. Each has a health check; `up` runs `docker compose up --detach --wait`, so it returns only when all four are healthy. Caddy waits for the object store and mail to be healthy. (3) **HTTPS:** Caddy's internal CA (`local_certs`, `skip_install_trust`: it never touches the machine's trust store) serves `adms.localhost` (the health page, `/health` → `200 ok`), `s3.adms.localhost` (the object store) and `mail.adms.localhost` (the mail inbox), with HSTS, `nosniff`, `no-referrer` and no `Server` header; HTTP/3 is off because only TCP is published. **Plain HTTP on port 80 is redirected (308) to HTTPS**; plain HTTP to 443 gets 400. `up` copies Caddy's **public** root certificate to `infra/local/.generated/caddy-root.crt` (git-ignored) for `curl --cacert` and browsers, then checks the health page over verified HTTPS itself. The API and web apps get their own hostnames when they're built. (4) **Ports, loopback only:** Caddy `127.0.0.1:443` and `:80`; Postgres `127.0.0.1:55432` (**not 5432**: a Homebrew Postgres and the historical stack already hold it on this machine); the mail catcher's SMTP `127.0.0.1:1025`. The object store publishes nothing: S3 is reached only through Caddy, over HTTPS. Each port can be changed in `.env` (`ADMS_HTTPS_PORT`, `ADMS_HTTP_PORT`, `ADMS_PG_PORT`, `ADMS_SMTP_PORT`). (5) **Dev secrets:** on a first run `up` generates `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` (32 random bytes), `S3_ACCESS_KEY` (20 characters) and `S3_SECRET_KEY` (30 random bytes) into **`infra/local/.env`**, git-ignored by `**/.env`, mode 0600, created exclusively; it never prints them. They reach the containers **as files, not environment variables**: Postgres through a compose secret (`POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`), SeaweedFS through a config file owned by its own user, mode 0400. `docker inspect` of every container holds none of the three values (checked). If `.env` is gone but the data volumes remain, `up` stops and says to run `local:wipe`, instead of making passwords that won't open the data. (6) **Lifecycle:** `down` removes the containers and the network and **keeps the data volumes** (a resume keeps `.env` and the data, checked); `wipe` also removes the volumes, `.env` and the root certificate, so the next `up` is a first run. The installer (0.2.4) builds on this. (7) **Hardening:** `no-new-privileges` on every container; the mail catcher runs as `nobody` with every capability dropped and its update check off; SeaweedFS telemetry **off** (it's on by default), its WebDAV, admin UI, Iceberg and Lance listeners off, **CORS by exact allow-list** (`https://adms.localhost`, widened when the web apps arrive), deleting a non-empty bucket refused. Postgres uses SCRAM-SHA-256. (8) **Known limitation (SeaweedFS 4.47):** with versioning **on**, a non-empty bucket **can** be deleted with its objects despite `-s3.allowDeleteBucketNotEmpty=false` (seen: 204, then 404 on the object). Without versioning it's refused (409, seen). The cause is upstream: its emptiness check skips entries ending in `.versions`, where a versioned bucket keeps its objects (the code is quoted in seaweedfs#11490/#11491). It's a local-dev store, and "nothing is lost" never rests on the store: the API's S3 identity will have no bucket-delete permission when media arrives (Phase 2/3). Reporting it upstream is the user's call. **Agent defaults** (ADR-230): the hostnames, port 55432, `down` keeping data, the helper's command names. | Answers BACKLOG 0.2.3; REQ-006 met for today's services. |

| **ADR-266** | 2026-09-29 | Scaffold / installer | ⚠️ **AMENDED BY ADR-281** — the master passcode's hash is kept only in the database (never in `packages/db/.env`), and a resume after the database was lost asks for the passcode again. **The installer is `pnpm installer` (with `installer:check` and `installer:teardown`): a three-question interview, secrets made only on a first run, the four login roles and the database, then migrations and the seed (stubs until 0.3)** (BACKLOG 0.2.4, REQ-007, REQ-008). (1) **The name:** `pnpm setup` is pnpm's own command (it edits the shell profile), so a root script called `setup` is a trap; **`installer`** is used instead, beside `local:*`. Code: `tools/setup/src/` (`Installer`, `Interview`, `Database`, `EnvFile`, `InstallationState`, `SecretMaker`, `ScramVerifier`, `PasscodeHasher`), class-style, run by Node 24 as-is. (2) **First run:** brings the local stack up if it isn't (ADR-263), refuses if it finds env files, logins or the database with no installation record (their secrets can't be trusted; says to tear down), then asks (a) **the firm's name**, (b) **email through the local mail catcher, or none** (ADR-170: without email, admins reset passwords), (c) **the master passcode**, typed twice, never shown (ADR-106). Then one confirm. (3) **Secrets, made once:** a 256-bit password for each login and a 256-bit **`ADMS_TOKEN_SIGNING_SECRET`** for the API (its use is Phase 2's to decide); the master passcode is kept only as an **Argon2id** hash (19 MiB, 2 passes, 1 lane: OWASP's first setting; PHC string) from **Node 24's own `crypto.argon2`** (stable, added v24.7.0; no dependency). **One env file per service, each with only its own logins** (REQ-008): `packages/db/.env` (`adms_owner`, for migrations and the seed; the passcode hash until the seed can move it into the database), `apps/api/.env` (`adms_api`, `adms_readonly` for the portal's queries, the token secret, `SMTP_URL`), `apps/worker/.env` (`adms_worker`). Each is **created exclusively, mode 0600**, git-ignored by `**/.env`, so no run can overwrite a secret. The **installation record** `tools/setup/.state/installation.json` (git-ignored) holds no secret: firm, email, host, port, database, when each step ran. (4) **Database:** four `LOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOREPLICATION NOBYPASSRLS` roles (ARCHITECTURE §5.1), each created with a **SCRAM-SHA-256 verifier made by the installer**, so no password ever reaches the server or its log; database **`adms`**, owned by `adms_owner`, `CONNECT` revoked from `PUBLIC` and granted to the other three. Table grants, the guards and row-level security are 0.3's migrations, not the installer's. Then each login is proven to open `adms` with its own password. **Migrations and the seed** print that there's nothing yet and run on every run (idempotent) once 0.3 fills them. (5) **Rerun:** says what it knows (never a secret), re-checks it (the stack answers; each env file there and owner-only; the passcode hash well formed; each login exists; the database's owner; nobody else may connect; each login opens it), asks **once**: resume? On yes it puts back what it can **with the secrets it has** (a lost database gets its logins back with the same passwords); **a missing secret stops it** (it never remakes one), pointing to teardown. On no, nothing changes. `--yes` answers the confirms (a first run still needs its answers, one per line on standard input). What existed: ADR-160 and ADR-188 allow firm-added fields on surveys, ROE forms, incidents and drop-off logs ("a form definition … plus stored answers") and left the storage shape to `spec/DATA-MODEL.md`, not yet drafted; the schema's only JSON columns are `AuditRecord`'s prior and new values. **The path** (the direction is the user's; the details below are an *agent default* that `spec/DATA-MODEL.md` settles): (1) **The boundary stands (ADR-160):** anything that bills keeps fixed, typed columns; flexible data is allowed only where the engine, the rules and the flags never read it. A value they must one day read is **promoted to a real column by a migration**, never read out of JSONB. (2) **A form definition** per record kind: fields each with a stable ID, a label, a type (text, number, yes/no, pick from a list, photo) and whether it's required. A change makes a **new version**; a version is never edited or deleted (as map versions are, ADR-141). (3) **Each record holds one JSONB answers column**, an object keyed by field ID, **and the definition version it was answered against**. A photo answer holds the photo record's ID, never the file (ARCHITECTURE §11). (4) **Checked by one schema generated from the definition**, in `packages/contracts`, the same on the phone, the API and the web; unknown keys are rejected (ARCHITECTURE §6). (5) **Corrected and audited like any captured field** (ADR-051, 097): the database's audit capture already keeps prior and new values as JSON. (6) **Through Prisma's `Json` type** (jsonb in Postgres) and its JSON filters, no hand-written SQL (ADR-094); an index on the answers only when a real query needs one; exports flatten answers into columns by field label. (7) **Extending later is a definition change, not a migration:** a new field, or a new field type added to the schema generator. Opening added fields on another kind of record is a new decision, and (1) travels with it. **Not decided here:** whether `Device` carries a details column of this kind (0.4.3's call, C37); the promo's other claims (PostGIS, Valkey) stay as ARCHITECTURE §3 has them. | ADR-160's "stored answers" has a shape to draft from; `spec/DATA-MODEL.md` (0.2b.2) settles names and may overturn the details (C36). No rule, check or price ever depends on a JSONB value. |

| **ADR-301** | 2026-10-02 | Pay items / rules | **A pay item's code is unique on its project; a pay item is its code and its description, both the firm's own; an exact duplicate of a rule is refused before it is saved.** The user, reading acceptance scenario AC-01-41 ("neither a code nor a name is unique"), found that ADR-147 had recorded their answer to Q-139 the wrong way round. The question had asked "may two service codes on a project share the name `3A`, or should the second be named e.g. `3A-2`?" and the answer began "Yes"; the agent took it for the first half. **User, 2026-10-02, the corrected answer in `spec/QUESTIONS.md` (as a firm setting up):** "Yes (the second should be named e.g. `3A-2`) but we don't want to make anything that forces this onto the firm - we dont want to force this `3A-2` prefix naming - we want to let them decide what to nme it. So if we already have a transaction in slot 1 a ticket and then we get another for it in the same slot, we'd know it's likely an issue and flag it. This way allows for more flexibility on the firm side to set things up how they need to use it, vs ridgid setup on on dev side." **And in chat:** "The "code" is the number+chars you assign it. This must be unique per project. We would expect that "code" to have a description so we know what the work was for. And when we create a rule we want to name that rule something that matches to the payitem."; "The code should be unique, but the decription should be whatever the firm wants to make it."; on the duplicate: "Exact dup check is ideal. We'd want to make it a check that runs before the new rule is saved. User would want to see an error noting what the issue is so they dont waste more time working."; on the agent's phrase "the contract's words and line number": "i dont like hearing line number like that". (1) **The code is unique on its project.** The firm types every code; setup still only suggests one from the convention (ADR-235) and forces no pattern, for a second pay item or any other. A rate that changes from a date is a second pay item with a code of its own (the firm's choice; the examples use `VEG-HAUL-CY-15-B`) and *Ticket date* criteria on the two rules; editing a rate stays the way to fix a mistake (ADR-090). The database refuses a second pay item with a code its project already has (a unique key on project and code). *Agent defaults:* an archived pay item keeps its code, so it can't be taken again (old tickets and the audit log still name it); codes are compared exactly as typed; another project may use the same code. (2) **A pay item has two texts, not three: its code and its description.** The legacy screen's separate name (ADR-207) is gone: the monitor's list shows the payable type, never a pay item's name (ADR-213), so the name had no job the description doesn't do. The description is whatever the firm wants to say about the work ("ROW VEG haul 0–15 mi"); it is shown with the code wherever a pay item is listed or exported, and nothing reads it. *Agent default:* it is required ("we would expect that code to have a description"), and two pay items may have the same description. **The phrase "the contract's words and line number" is withdrawn everywhere**: it was the agent's (ADR-235), never the user's, and its "Line 3" example was made up. (3) **A rule's name stays the firm's free text**; naming it to match its pay item is the firm's practice, and a rule the pay item screen's "Pays when" writes is named from its pay item's code and description (agent default). (4) **An exact duplicate of a rule is refused before it is saved**, with an error that names the rule it duplicates, so nobody builds on it. *The details are an agent default:* two rules are the same when they are on the same form, name the same contract (or both none), and have the same criteria (criterion, operator and values, in any order) and the same actions (kind, #, pay item, *Quantity from* and its chosen items, in any order); the rule's name and its Active tick are ignored; it is compared with every rule of the project that isn't archived, inactive ones included; an edit that would turn a rule into a copy of another is refused the same way; the wording is "Not saved: this rule is the same as "<the other rule's name>"." | **ADR-310** | 2026-10-02 | Database / dependency | **The `btree_gist` extension is added, so the database itself refuses overlapping size bands** (ADR-309 (7) had left it to setup alone, for want of the extension). **User, 2026-10-02:** "i saw adr 309 and agree we would want to add that extenstion". (1) **What:** `btree_gist` **1.8**, PostgreSQL's own contrib module (the PostgreSQL licence, maintained with Postgres itself), the version Postgres 18 ships, pinned in the migration (`CREATE EXTENSION "btree_gist" WITH SCHEMA "extensions" VERSION '1.8'`). It is **trusted**, so `adms_owner` installs it without a superuser (no login gains a power; `grants.test.ts` unchanged on that). (2) **Where:** a schema of its own, **`extensions`**, owned by `adms_owner`, with **no right for `PUBLIC` or any runtime login**. Its C functions are callable by anyone by default, pin no search path and belong to the bootstrap superuser; in `public` they would break three standing guards (every `public` function the owner's, its search path pinned, none callable but the five granted). An index calls them without the right, so `adms_api` writes pay items as before (tried as `adms_api` on a throw-away copy before it was applied). (3) **The guard:** `pay_item_bands_never_overlap`, an exclusion constraint: on one project, two pay items of one payable type, neither archived, never have bands that share a tenth of an inch (`numrange(band_from, band_to, '[]')`, an open end unbounded), exactly `SizeBands`' rule; a pay item with no band takes no part, and an archived one can't be put back over a band that took its place. Setup's words stay `SizeBands`' (AC-01-45 at the domain); the database is the backstop (`23P01`). (4) **Prisma:** its shadow database is emptied schema `public` only, so the `extensions` schema survived a reset and the migration failed on replay (`schema "extensions" already exists`, P3006, seen 2026-10-02). `packages/db/prisma.config.js` now drops it there first (`migrations.initShadowDb`, which Prisma offers only under `experimental.externalTables`; no table is named external, so nothing else changes). `prisma migrate diff` from the database to the schema is empty: Prisma doesn't see the constraint or the extension, so it never proposes dropping either. (5) **Also open to C43:** number blocks of one series never overlapping (task 1.3.2) can now use the same idiom, with no ADR of its own for the extension. | The 33rd migration (`guard_size_bands_never_overlap`). `grants.test.ts`: the extension and its schema exactly; `catalog.test.ts`: every exclusion constraint exactly; `pay-items.test.ts`: the database's half of AC-01-45. A cloud Postgres must offer `btree_gist` 1.8 (every major managed Postgres 18 does; recorded for the deploy, Phase 5).

Either way the quarantined record stays, marked with who, when and the domain's words; a second resolution is refused. (6) **A renumber (08 point 11)** changes the ticket number, a split collection's suffix, or both, on one field event; a whole ticket is each of its field events in turn. It is refused only what can't be a number: a blank, the number it has, a suffix that isn't capital letters or sits on a kind that takes none, and a number another field event of its kind holds (the database's own key, caught and told in plain words; invariant 17). Whether the work is real is never asked (ADR-028, 051; AC-08-30). **A renumber of a field event of a voided ticket is not decided here** (C78): it changes the number and nothing else, and what a void does under a new number is settled with the worker reading `TicketVoid`, task 1.8.4 (08 point 6). Told that holding lockout only in the API process falls short of NIST SP 800-63B (it is forgotten at a restart and not shared by two processes), that mainstream products keep a failed-try count and a lock on the account's own record, and that failed sign-ins kept only in a log are weaker evidence than the audit log: "Then we should revert the change we just made so that it aligns with the better outline of the standard and make sure to adhere to it in the future. (1) **Reverted.** The schema, the tests, `spec/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `spec/DATA-MODEL.md`, `spec/THREAT-MODEL.md`, acceptance file 10, REQ-202b and both skills are as committed at `9377b04` (written back from that commit's content; no git state changed). `SecurityEventKind` has `SIGN_IN_FAILED` and `LOCKOUT` again and `UserCredential` its `lockedUntil`. (2) **The standard, for 2.2.3 and every later task of sign-in:** tries against a real account are limited by state that outlasts a restart and is shared by every API process, so it is kept in the database on that person's sign-in record (`lockedUntil`; where the count lives is 2.2.3's, C88); a failed sign-in and a lockout are in the audit log's security domain, as ARCHITECTURE §6 and REQ-202b say. (3) **What stays of the user's concern, as an agent default for 2.2.3 to build and test:** the database never grows at a stranger's will and never holds what a stranger typed. A try at a name nobody has writes no row (one log line); no typed name, password or code is ever stored; and writes for a real account are bounded by the lockout itself (once it is locked, further tries add nothing until it opens). Rate limits (2.2.6) bound the rest. (4) **Open again, as ADR-399 (5) left it:** who is stated as the actor of the write a failed try causes (every write needs a real actor, and only the worker states the system actor, ADR-276): 2.2.3, and 2.5.1 for the master passcode (REQ-209). (5) **How to work, from now on:** when the user, or anyone, suggests a direction in security, check it against the named standards and say what they ask and what comparable products do **before** building it; build a departure only once the user has heard that and still chooses it, recorded as an accepted risk. ADR-420's row, the roadmap and `SUMMARY.md` are reworded: "a certification that arrives from a phone", never "made on a phone … as a sync does". *Not asked, left open:* the warning's words and the screen (Phase 3's design). | When the number at New isn't in the phone's list of certifications, the phone warns, asks to refresh its lists if it has a connection, and otherwise lets the monitor key the truck in by hand (ADR-154). Certifying happens where there is signal (ADR-151); ADR-420 (6)'s wording corrected. Phase 3 builds it (REQ-317) |

(2) **What this part puts behind a request and what it leaves (never widened).** Behind a request: a measuring mistake corrected (`Corrections.certification`), signatures on file (`Certifications.signaturesOnFile`), a revocation (`Certifications.revoke`). **Left: a certification made, and a modified truck certified again ("replaced"), which is the same call naming the one it replaces.** Certifying is done by a monitor on a phone whose assignment includes it (ADR-151, 240), so both arrive through the phone's sync (task 2.6.2, BACKLOG C62); nothing recorded lets the back office make a certification, and none was inferred. Its QC status is `setQcStatus`'s (ADR-430) and the merge of a sub is setup's (ADR-426). (3) **Each service asks again inside its own piece of work.** `Certifications` now stands on `ReviewService`: `signaturesOnFile` asks *QC* (it is marked at QC, ADR-080; before, it asked nothing), and `revoke` asks the domain's new `CertificationChanges.revoker`, which lets an admin in service through and nobody else, a manager/analyst who holds every permission included ("Luis Ortega may not revoke certification 730415: it takes an admin. (4) **A measuring correction's body** is `changes` (any of `length`, `secondLength`, `width`, `height`, `diameter`, `radius`, `run`, `corners`; whole inches of 1 or more, at least one stated) and the reviewer's note, **which `Corrections.certification` now takes and the audit log keeps** (it took none). (7) **The answer** (`certificationRecordSchema`): the certification as it stands (number, kind, prime and subs, capacity, when and by whom certified, signatures on file, what it replaces, the revocation's day, reason and admin). **Never the driver's phone or licence number**, which no change here reads or moves. (9) Seen: 121 test files, 2,342 tests (`apps/api/test/certifications.test.ts`, 8; two more in `packages/domain/test/certifications.test.ts`); six loosenings (a revocation that asks nobody, signatures asking *correct*, a correction asking *QC*, the note dropped, the revocation opened to the whole back office, the answer's count dropped), six caught; lint clean; 421 licences; 17 stories; `pnpm security` 7 passed. | **ADR-436** | 2026-10-09 | Phones / enrolment and a phone's proof of itself: what the standards ask, and the task cut in three *(task 2.5.1; the user's word of ADR-401: said before building; read on 2026-10-09 at pages.nist.gov/800-63-4 (SP 800-63B-4) and in OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 chapters V6 and V11)* | **(1) What NIST SP 800-63B-4 asks of a device key** (§3.1.6, single-factor cryptographic authentication): the key and its algorithm give at least the minimum security strength (112 bits today, §3.1.6.2); a non-exportable key is kept in an isolated execution environment (§3.1.6.1; non-exportable keys are *required* only at AAL3, §3.2.13); the verifier's challenge nonce is at least 64 bits and unique, or made by an approved random bit generator (§3.1.6.2, §3.2.12); verification uses approved cryptography; the protocol is replay-resistant (§3.2.7: a recorded authentication message replayed must not succeed); the verifier's keys are protected against modification, and a public key needs no secrecy. A session secret that follows an authentication is made by the server in direct response to it, with at least 64 random bits, sent only over the protected channel, and times out (§5.1). **(2) What ASVS 5.0 asks:** 6.7.2 (a challenge nonce of at least 64 bits, unique; Level 3), 11.2.3 (at least 128 bits of security, Level 2), 11.5.1 (random values from a CSPRNG with at least 128 bits of entropy), 11.6.1 (approved algorithms for signature generation and verification), 6.1.1 and 6.3.1 (the controls against brute force are documented, built as documented, and keep a stranger from locking an account out). **(3) What they ask of a passcode:** kept only as a salted, slow hash; never one known from breaches; no composition rule, no forced change (§3.1.1.2); consecutive wrong tries limited, to no more than 100, by disabling the authenticator, which is then bound again before it is used (§3.2.2). **(4) What neither provides for, said as a standing departure:** a secret shared by several people. Nothing in this task widens it. **Also said:** attestation was declined (ADR-240), so the server takes a phone's word that its key is in secure hardware; 800-63B does not ask for attestation at this level. **(5) The cut, three parts, one a response.** *Part 1 (ADR-437, done):* the key's kind, the challenge and what a phone signs, as rules and classes with their tests; nothing wired, no endpoint, no table. *Part 2:* the database's share and enrolment: who the record names for an act under the master passcode (C45), wrong tries at it (ADR-438 is the proposal, the user's to overturn before it is built), `POST` enrolment with the passcode checked with back-off, the public key kept, the security events, the log read (AC-10-22, 44; AC-02-18's first half; AC-10-32's enrolment). *Part 3:* the challenge asked for and answered, good once on the phone's own record, a phone's short-lived token and `Admission`'s access for a proven phone, a revoked key refused, the harness's phone with a software key and the stories enrolling through the service (AC-05-03, AC-10-45, 46; AC-02-18 whole at the API). | Say what the standard asks, then build to it. The master passcode's sharing is ADR-106's accepted risk, restated. Task 2.5.1 is three parts |

| **ADR-438** | 2026-10-09 | Phones / who the record names for an act under the master passcode, and wrong tries at it *(task 2.5.1, part 2's design; BACKLOG C45, C88, C90, C93; REQ-209; AC-10-22; **PROPOSED, agent default: not built; the user's to overturn before part 2 builds it**, because it decides what the audit log says)* | **(1) The record names the master passcode itself, never a person.** The passcode isn't a user and whoever holds it is not known, by ADR-106 and ADR-240. (c) **The browser test build keeps it in IndexedDB**, against 14.3.3: for testing only, never real work (ARCHITECTURE §8). So when a monitor's password is set, and at an online sign-in where there is none yet, the server also keeps **an offline seed**: Argon2id of the password under a salt of its own, with no key, **sealed at rest as an authenticator's secret is** (ADR-412) and kept out of the audit log. **A phone's entry is Argon2id of that seed under a salt unique to that phone and monitor.** The phone is sent the seed's salt and settings, the entry's salt and the entry, never the seed; it checks a typed password by doing both steps. (b) **Who is on a phone's list:** the monitor signed in and every monitor not archived who has an assignment that stands on that project for its today or later; ARCHITECTURE §7.1's "each monitor enabled on that project" has no record of its own. (c) **The master passcode's check is made the same way from the server's own hash**, which therefore stays unkeyed (C90, C110 answered): the phone is sent that hash's salt and settings, a salt of the phone's own and Argon2id of the hash under it, with the passcode's version; `Device.masterPasscodeVersion` moves when the phone is sent it, written as the device key's actor.
